title: the Tenga, Spirits of the Earth
summary: The Mossi people believe the earth is alive with spirits called Tenga who must be consulted before every harvest — and those who ignore them find their fields barren and their children sick.
full_text:
The Mossi people of Burkina Faso do not own the land. No one owns the land. The land owns itself, and the Tenga are its voice.

The Tenga are the spirits of the earth. They are not gods — the Mossi have gods, and the Tenga are not among them. They are not ancestors — the Mossi have ancestors, and the Tenga are older than any ancestor. The Tenga are the earth itself, speaking through the soil, through the rocks, through the roots of the baobab trees.

Before the Mossi plant, they consult the Tenga. A farmer does not simply stick seeds in the ground and hope for rain. He goes to the earth priest — the teng-wobde — and asks permission. The teng-wobde pours a libation of millet beer on the ground. He speaks to the earth. He asks the Tenga: Is this the right time? Is this the right place? Is this the right crop?

The Tenga answer. Not in words — the earth does not speak in words. The Tenga answer in signs: a bird landing on a specific tree, a snake crossing the path, the direction of the wind. The teng-wobde reads these signs and tells the farmer: Plant here. Plant now. Plant this.

The farmer obeys. He plants. The earth receives the seeds. The Tenga tend them, pushing water through the roots, pulling nutrients from the soil, sheltering the young plants from the wind.

But if a farmer plants without consulting the Tenga — if he is impatient, or arrogant, or simply forgetful — the Tenga are offended. Not angry — the earth does not get angry. The Tenga are offended the way the soil is offended when you plant the wrong seed in the wrong place: with a quiet, implacable resistance.

The farmer's crops do not grow. The seeds germinate, but the shoots are thin and pale. The rain falls, but the water runs off the soil instead of soaking in. The harvest is small — smaller than it should be, smaller than the farmer's neighbors' harvest.

And sometimes, the Tenga take more than a harvest. Sometimes, they take health. A farmer who repeatedly ignores the Tenga finds his children falling sick — not with the diseases that sweep through villages, but with the old sicknesses, the ones that have no name, the ones that make the body waste away slowly.

The only cure is to return to the teng-wobde, to pour a libation on the ground, to ask the Tenga for forgiveness. The Tenga forgive — the earth always forgives, if you ask. But the forgiveness is slow. It takes time. It takes seasons. It takes the patient work of a farmer who has learned that the land is not a thing to be used, but a spirit to be consulted.

The Mossi say: The Tenga were here before us. They will be here after us. We do not own the land. We borrow it, and the rent is respect.
moral: The land does not belong to those who farm it. It belongs to itself, and the rent is respect.
source: Mossi oral tradition, documented by Paul Pascal Coulibaly

title: the Karanga, the Diviner's Secret
summary: A sorcerer who reads the future in the patterns of millet flour scattered on water — but the future he reads is not the one you want to hear.
full_text:
The Karanga is the diviner of the Mossi people. He is not a witch — witches take without asking. He is not a priest — priests speak to gods. The Karanga speaks to the patterns.

When a farmer cannot find his cattle, when a woman cannot conceive, when a child falls sick with no fever and no cough, they go to the Karanga. The Karanga lives in a small hut at the edge of the village, where the grass is long and the path is narrow.

The Karanga does not ask questions. He sits behind a screen of woven grass, and the person who comes to him places a gift at the foot of the screen: a chicken, a bag of millet, a piece of cloth. The gift is not payment. The gift is a signal — it tells the Karanga that the person is serious, that they are ready to hear what the patterns say.

The Karanga takes a handful of millet flour and scatters it on the surface of a bowl of water. He watches the patterns the flour makes — the swirls, the clumps, the spaces between. He reads the patterns the way a farmer reads the sky: for signs, for warnings, for the direction of the wind.

The patterns tell the future. But the future is not what the person wants to hear.

The patterns say: Your cattle are not lost. They were stolen by your brother's wife, who is jealous of your herd.

The patterns say: You will conceive, but not until the dry season, and the child will be difficult.

The patterns say: Your child is not sick with a disease. Your child is sick with a curse, placed by the woman who lives at the edge of the village, the one who smiles too much.

The Karanga tells the truth. He does not soften it. He does not wrap it in polite words. He tells the truth the way the patterns show it — sharp, clear, and uncomfortable.

Some people leave the Karanga's hut angry. They say the Karanga is a liar, a fraud, a man who makes up stories to scare people. They say the millet flour is just millet flour, and the water is just water.

But the patterns are never wrong. The cattle are always where the patterns say they are. The child is always sick for the reasons the patterns give. The future unfolds the way the patterns show it — not because the Karanga is a prophet, but because the patterns reveal what is already true.

The Karanga does not make predictions. He reads the truth that is already there, hidden in the flour, in the water, in the swirls and clumps and spaces. The truth is always there. Most people just do not know how to read it.
moral: The truth is always there. Most people just do not know how to read it.

title: the Keemse, Spirit of the River
summary: A water spirit that lives in the deep pools of the Volta River, granting fish to those who respect it — and drowning those who do not.
full_text:
The Volta River is the life of Burkina Faso. Its water feeds the fields, its fish feed the people, its current carries the canoes that connect village to village. But the Volta has a spirit, and the spirit has moods.

The Keemse lives in the deep pools — the places where the river slows and darkens and the bottom disappears into black water. The Keemse is not visible. It does not appear as a shape or a figure or a face. The Keemse appears as a feeling — the feeling of being watched from beneath the surface, the feeling of water moving where there is no current, the feeling of something large and old turning its attention toward you.

Fishermen know the Keemse. They respect it. Before they cast their nets, they pour a libation of millet beer into the water. They speak to the Keemse: We are guests in your house. We take only what we need. We leave the rest.

The Keemse hears. If the fisherman is sincere — if he takes only what he needs, if he does not use nets with mesh too fine to let the young fish escape — the Keemse grants him fish. The fish are fat and plentiful. The nets are heavy. The canoe rides low in the water.

But if the fisherman is greedy — if he takes more than he needs, if he uses nets that catch the young and the old alike, if he pours nothing into the water — the Keemse takes offense. Not anger — the Keemse does not get angry. The Keemse takes offense the way the river takes offense when you dam it: by finding another path.

The fisherman's nets come up empty. The deep pools, which were teeming with fish yesterday, are empty today. The river moves to another part of the bank, leaving the fisherman stranded on dry land.

And sometimes, the Keemse takes more than fish. Sometimes, a fisherman who has offended the Keemse falls from his canoe into the deep pool. The water is cold. The current is strong. The Keemse pulls him down — not violently, not quickly, but slowly, gently, the way the river pulls a leaf into its current.

The fisherman does not come back. His canoe is found drifting downstream. His nets are tangled. The river is quiet.

The Mossi say that the Keemse is not a spirit of punishment. It is a spirit of balance. The river gives fish, and the fisherman must give respect. If the balance is kept, the river gives generously. If the balance is broken, the river takes.

The Volta flows on. The Keemse waits in the deep pools. The fishermen cast their nets and pour their libations and hope that the balance is kept.
moral: The river gives generously, but only to those who give respect in return.

title: the Gu, Guardian of the Crossing
summary: A sacred crocodile that guards the river crossing, granting safe passage to those who show respect — and dragging beneath the water those who do not.
full_text:
The Gu is the crocodile of the sacred pool.

It lives in a pool on the outskirts of the village — not the village pool, not the one where the women wash clothes and the children play. The sacred pool, the one that is surrounded by trees and silence, the one where no one goes without permission.

The Gu is large. Its body is the length of three men laid end to end. Its scales are the color of the earth after rain — dark, rich, glistening. Its eyes are yellow, and they catch the light the way a mirror catches it — suddenly, brilliantly, without warning.

The Gu is not a wild animal. It is a guardian. It guards the crossing — the place where the path meets the water, where the village meets the forest, where the living meet the dead. Every village has a crossing, and every crossing has a Gu.

When a person needs to cross — to visit a neighbor, to attend a ceremony, to follow a path that leads through the water — they approach the Gu with respect. They bring an offering: a chicken, a piece of kola nut, a calabash of millet beer. They place the offering at the water's edge and step back.

The Gu considers. It does not move quickly — crocodiles are not quick to decide. It watches the person with its yellow eyes. It smells the offering. It feels the vibrations of the person's heartbeat through the water.

If the person is sincere — if they have come in peace, if they carry no malice, if they intend no harm to the crossing — the Gu slides into the water. The path across the pool becomes clear. The water is calm. The person crosses.

If the person is not sincere — if they carry weapons, if they intend to steal, if they cross with hatred in their hearts — the Gu does not move. The path remains closed. The water is rough. The person cannot cross.

And sometimes, if the person is very insistent — if they try to force the crossing, if they wade into the water without permission — the Gu surfaces. It rises from the deep, its body filling the width of the pool, its mouth open, its teeth white against the dark water.

The person does not cross. The person does not come back.

The Mossi say that the Gu has guarded the crossing for as long as the village has existed. It is older than the oldest tree. It is larger than the largest canoe. It remembers every person who has crossed, every offering that has been made, every offense that has been committed.

The Gu is not a spirit of fear. It is a spirit of boundaries. It guards the line between here and there, between us and them, between the living and the dead. Without the Gu, the boundaries would dissolve, and the world would be a place without edges.

The crossing remains. The Gu waits. The offerings are made. The path is kept.
moral: Every boundary has a guardian, and every guardian demands respect.
source: Mossi sacred tradition, documented by Germain Rongier

title: the Kinkirsi, the Human Animal
summary: A being that is half-human, half-animal, born when a mother's craving during pregnancy crosses the boundary between species — and lives forever in the forest, caught between two worlds.
full_text:
The Kinkirsi is born from craving.

The Mossi believe that when a woman is pregnant, her cravings are not random. They are messages — from the unborn child, from the spirits, from the earth itself. A craving for millet porridge means the child will love the village. A craving for honey means the child will love the forest. A craving for a specific animal's meat means the child will carry that animal's spirit.

But some cravings are too strong. Some cravings cross the boundary between human and animal. A woman who craves the meat of a leopard — not the taste of it, but the power of it, the speed of it, the way it moves through the forest without making a sound — may give birth to a Kinkirsi.

The Kinkirsi is a child that is not entirely a child. It has a human face, but its body is covered in fur. It has human hands, but its feet are paws. It has a human voice, but it speaks in the growls and whines of the animal whose spirit it carries.

The Kinkirsi does not stay in the village. It cannot. The village is too small for a being that is caught between two worlds. The Kinkirsi runs to the forest, where the trees are tall and the light is green and the animals do not ask questions about what it is.

In the forest, the Kinkirsi lives as the animal lives. It hunts. It sleeps in the hollows of trees. It drinks from streams. But it never forgets that it was born from a human mother, and it never stops wanting to return to the village.

The Kinkirsi appears at the edge of the forest, at dusk, when the shadows are long and the light is fading. It watches the village from behind the trees. It watches the women cooking, the children playing, the men sitting by the fire. It wants to join them. It wants to sit by the fire and eat millet porridge and hear the stories.

But it cannot. The village would not accept it. The children would scream. The men would reach for their bows. The women would cover their eyes.

The Kinkirsi is not dangerous. It is lonely. It is a being that belongs to two worlds and belongs to neither. It carries the spirit of an animal and the memory of a mother, and it cannot reconcile them.

The Mossi say that the Kinkirsi is a lesson. A lesson about the boundaries between species, between human and animal, between village and forest. A lesson about the power of craving, and the consequences of desire.

The Kinkirsi is still in the forest. It is still watching the village from behind the trees. It is still waiting for someone to invite it to sit by the fire.
moral: Some beings belong to two worlds and neither world will have them.

title: the Kintogou, the Fire Serpent
summary: A serpent made of fire that coils beneath the village, its heat warming the earth in winter and its rage burning the village in summer — because fire is a gift, but it is never free.
full_text:
The Kintogou is the fire that lives beneath the village.

It is not a fire that you can see. It is not a fire that you can cook with or warm yourself by. It is a fire that you can feel — a deep, slow heat that rises from the ground in the dry season, warming the soil, warming the roots of the trees, warming the water in the wells.

The Mossi say that the Kintogou is a serpent. Not a real serpent — a serpent made of fire, coiled beneath the earth, its body running through the rock and the soil like a root. Its head is beneath the center of the village, where the chief's hut stands. Its tail is beneath the forest, where the trees are tallest.

The Kintogou gives heat. In the cold season, when the harmattan wind blows from the Sahara and the nights are long and freezing, the Kintogou warms the village. The ground is warm beneath the feet. The water in the wells is not cold. The children sleep without shivering.

But the Kintogou demands respect. It demands that the village maintain the balance — that the chief performs the rituals, that the priests pour the libations, that the people do not take more fire than they need.

When the balance is maintained, the Kintogou gives heat gently, the way a mother holds a child. When the balance is broken — when the rituals are skipped, when the offerings are forgotten, when the people grow greedy — the Kintogou gives heat the way a fire gives heat: without mercy.

The ground cracks. The wells dry up. The trees catch fire. The huts burn. The village is consumed.

The Mossi tell the story of the village that forgot the Kintogou. The chief stopped performing the rituals. The priests stopped pouring the libations. The people stopped leaving offerings at the center of the village, where the Kintogou's head was said to be.

The Kintogou waited. It is patient — fire is patient. It waited through one season, then another, then another. When the dry season came, and the harmattan blew, and the village was dry and brittle, the Kintogou rose.

The ground split open. Flames poured from the crack — not the yellow flames of a cooking fire, but the blue flames of something that burns without fuel. The village burned. The people fled. The chief's hut collapsed into ash.

When the fire was over, the village was gone. The crack in the ground closed. The Kintogou coiled back beneath the earth, its heat spent, its rage satisfied.

The Mossi rebuilt the village. They performed the rituals. They poured the libations. They left offerings at the center of the village, where the crack had been.

The Kintogou gave heat gently, the way a mother holds a child.

The Kintogou is still beneath the village. It is still coiled, still waiting, still giving heat. The Mossi still perform the rituals. They still pour the libations. They still leave offerings.

The fire is a gift. But it is never free.
moral: Fire is a gift, but it is never free. Respect the heat that warms you.

title: the Mba-Katrè, Spirit of the Divination Bowl
summary: A spirit that lives in the diviner's bowl, speaking through the patterns of cast cowrie shells — but it only tells the truth, never what you want to hear.
full_text:
The Mba-Katrè lives in the bowl.

Not a specific bowl — any bowl that a diviner uses for casting cowrie shells. But once the bowl is used, once the cowrie shells are cast into it for the first time, the Mba-Katrè enters. It lives in the curve of the bowl, in the shadow cast by the rim, in the space between the shells.

The Mba-Katrè is not a ghost. It is not a god. It is the spirit of truth — not truth as humans understand it, but truth as the cowrie shells show it. The truth that is already there, hidden in the patterns, waiting to be read.

When a person comes to the diviner, they place their question in the bowl. Not a spoken question — a physical one. A piece of their hair, a fragment of their clothing, a pinch of the earth from their doorstep. The Mba-Katrè reads the question from the object, and it answers.

The answer comes in the pattern of the cowrie shells. The diviner casts the shells into the bowl, and they fall where they will. The Mba-Katrè arranges them — not by moving them, but by choosing where they land. Each shell is a syllable. Each pattern is a sentence. Each arrangement is a truth.

The Mba-Katrè tells the truth. It does not soften it. It does not wrap it in comfortable words. It tells the truth the way the shells show it: directly, clearly, and without mercy.

The Mba-Katrè says: Your husband has another wife. She lives in the next village. She is carrying his child.

The Mba-Katrè says: Your harvest will fail this year. The rain will come late and leave early. The millet will wither.

The Mba-Katrè says: Your mother is not sick. Your mother is cursed. The curse was placed by the woman who lives across the river, the one who smiles when she sees you.

The person who hears the truth reacts in different ways. Some weep. Some rage. Some deny. Some accept.

The Mba-Katrè does not care how the person reacts. It has told the truth. The truth is now in the world. It cannot be taken back.

The diviner who carries the Mba-Katrè in their bowl is not a prophet. They are a translator. They translate the language of the shells into the language of humans. They do not make the truth — they only read it.

The Mba-Katrè is not a spirit of the past. It is a spirit of the present. It still lives in the diviner's bowl. It still tells the truth. It still does not care what you want to hear.

The cowrie shells are cast. The Mba-Katrè speaks. The truth is told.
moral: Truth does not ask permission. It simply arrives.
source: Mossi divination tradition, documented by Simplice Yéré

title: the Mba-Soêmba, Spirit of the Granary
summary: A spirit that protects the village granary, ensuring that the harvest lasts through the dry season — but only if the grain is shared equally.
full_text:
The Mba-Soêmba protects the granary.

In the Mossi villages, the granary is the most important building. It is larger than the chief's hut, stronger than the walls, more carefully built than any structure in the village. The granary holds the harvest — the millet, the sorghum, the fonio — the food that will keep the village alive through the dry season.

The Mba-Soêmba lives in the granary. It is not a visible spirit — you will not see it in the shadows, you will not hear it in the silence. The Mba-Soêmba is a presence, a weight, a feeling that the grain is being watched.

The Mba-Soêmba protects the grain from two threats: from the rats that gnaw through the walls, and from the humans who take more than their share.

The rats are easy. The Mba-Soêmba scares them away with sounds — the creak of a board, the rustle of grain, the snap of a twig. The rats flee. The grain is safe.

The humans are harder. The Mba-Soêmba cannot scare humans away — they are too large, too confident, too certain that the grain belongs to them. Instead, the Mba-Soêmba watches. It watches who takes grain from the granary, and how much they take.

When the grain is shared equally — when the chief distributes the harvest fairly, when no family takes more than they need, when the old and the young and the sick receive their portion — the Mba-Soêmba is content. The grain lasts. It stays fresh. It feeds the village through the dry season.

But when the grain is shared unequally — when the chief's family takes extra, when the strong take from the weak, when the hungry are told to wait — the Mba-Soêmba takes offense. The grain rots. It dries up. It disappears — not all at once, but slowly, so that the village does not notice until the hunger comes.

The Mossi say that the Mba-Soêmba is the spirit of fairness. It does not care about power, about status, about who is chief and who is farmer. It cares about one thing: that the grain is shared equally.

The chief who distributes the harvest fairly has the Mba-Soêmba's blessing. The granary is full. The village is fed. The dry season passes.

The chief who distributes the harvest unfairly has the Mba-Soêmba's curse. The granary empties. The village starves. The dry season does not end.

The Mba-Soêmba is still in the granary. It is still watching. It is still counting the grain.
moral: The spirit of the granary does not care about power. It cares about fairness.

title: the Sumbo, Spirit of the Fallow Field
summary: A spirit that inhabits the fields left fallow, protecting the land while it rests — and destroying anyone who plows a field before its rest is complete.
full_text:
The Sumbo lives in the fallow field.

The Mossi practice fallow farming — they plant a field for two or three years, then leave it fallow for five or six, letting the soil recover, letting the weeds grow, letting the earth rest. The fallow field is not empty. It is full of life — of grasses and bushes and the insects that feed on them, of the birds that feed on the insects, of the small animals that shelter in the undergrowth.

The Sumbo is the spirit of this rest. It lives in the tall grass, in the tangled bushes, in the dark spaces between the plants. It is not visible — you will not see it, even if you walk through the fallow field. The Sumbo is a presence, a feeling, a weight that settles on you when you enter a field that is not ready to be plowed.

The Sumbo protects the field while it rests. It ensures that the soil recovers, that the nutrients return, that the earth is ready to be planted again. The Sumbo works slowly — the way the soil works slowly, the way the roots work slowly, the way the earth rebuilds itself grain by grain.

If a farmer tries to plow a fallow field before its rest is complete — if he is impatient, if he is hungry, if he needs the land before it is ready — the Sumbo takes action. It does not attack. It does not curse. The Sumbo simply prevents the plow from turning the soil. The blade hits something hard beneath the surface — a root, a rock, something that should not be there. The oxen strain. The plow breaks. The farmer gives up.

And sometimes, the Sumbo does more. Sometimes, a farmer who repeatedly plows fallow fields before they are ready finds his crops failing — not because the soil is bad, but because the Sumbo has withdrawn its blessing. The soil looks rich. The soil looks ready. But the seeds do not grow. The plants are thin and pale. The harvest is nothing.

The Mossi say that the Sumbo is the spirit of patience. It teaches that the earth cannot be rushed. That rest is not emptiness. That a field left fallow is not a field wasted — it is a field healing.

The Sumbo is still in the fallow field. It is still resting. It is still waiting for the field to be ready.

The farmer waits. The soil recovers. The Sumbo blesses the field. The plow turns the earth. The seeds go in. The harvest comes.

But only when the field is ready.
moral: Rest is not emptiness. The earth heals in its own time.
source: Mossi agricultural tradition, Fada N'Gourma region

title: the Nyonyose, Spirit Behind the Mask
summary: When the mask dancer puts on the Nyonyose mask, the human disappears and the ancestor speaks — because in Burkina Faso, the dead do not leave, they wait behind the mask.
full_text:
The mask is not a mask.

When the dancer puts on the Nyonyose mask, he is not wearing a disguise. He is opening a door. The mask is the door between the living and the dead, between the present and the past, between the village and the ancestors.

The Nyonyose mask is carved from a single piece of wood — the wood of the balanzan tree, which grows slowly and lives for centuries. The carver who makes the mask does not carve it from a plan. He carves it from a vision — a dream, a feeling, a message from the ancestors that comes to him while he sleeps.

The mask is not beautiful. It is not meant to be beautiful. It is meant to be powerful. Its eyes are large and staring. Its mouth is open, as if speaking. Its surface is covered in scarification marks — the marks of the ancestors, the marks of the clan, the marks of the village.

When the dancer puts on the mask, he enters a trance. The ancestors enter through the mask. They take his body. They move his limbs. They speak with his voice. The dancer is gone — not dead, not unconscious, but absent. He has stepped aside to let the ancestors speak.

The ancestors speak of the village. They speak of the harvest, the drought, the birth, the death. They speak of the things the living have forgotten — the old ways, the old names, the old songs. They speak of the things the living need to remember.

The Nyonyose dance is not entertainment. It is a conversation. The villagers ask questions — not with words, but with gestures, with offerings, with the way they stand and sit and move. The ancestors answer — not with words, but with the dancer's body, with the rhythm of the drums, with the direction of the dance.

When the dance is over, the dancer removes the mask. He collapses. He sleeps. When he wakes, he does not remember the dance. He does not remember what the ancestors said. He does not remember anything — because the ancestors do not share their memories with the living.

The villagers remember. They carry the ancestors' words with them. They plant the crops the ancestors told them to plant. They avoid the places the ancestors warned them about. They sing the songs the ancestors taught them.

The Nyonyose mask is not a relic. It is not a museum piece. It is a living thing — a door that opens when the dancer puts it on, a voice that speaks when the ancestors enter, a bridge between the world that is and the world that was.

The mask waits. The ancestors wait. The dancer puts on the mask. The dead speak.
moral: The dead do not leave. They wait behind the mask, ready to speak.
